title: Atalanta and the Golden Apples
text:
Atalanta was faster than any man alive. An oracle had warned her against marriage, so she set a hard condition for her many suitors: each must race her. Whoever won would marry her, but whoever lost would die. Many tried, and all lost their lives.

Hippomenes came to watch one of these races, meaning to laugh at the fools who risked death for a bride. But when he saw Atalanta run, he fell in love and decided to challenge her himself. Before the race, he prayed to Venus for help. The goddess brought him three golden apples from her sacred garden on Cyprus and told him how to use them.

The race began, and Atalanta soon drew ahead. Hippomenes rolled the first golden apple across her path. Dazzled, she turned aside to pick it up, and he passed her. She caught up again. He threw the second, and again she stopped for it and lost ground, and again she overtook him.

Near the end, with the finish line close, Hippomenes threw the last apple off to the side of the course, with all his strength. Atalanta hesitated, then ran after it, and Venus made the apple heavier to slow her down. Hippomenes crossed the line first and won his bride.
lesson: A stronger competitor can be beaten by pulling them off course. Watch for shiny distractions that cost you the race you are actually running.
